title: ‘Tough-on-crime’ and the smaller ideas that work better
summary: More time behind bars does not mean better outcomes for inmates, who would be better served if Maryland worked to trim its prison population and use the savings for programs to help those incarcerated, writes Phil Caroom.
content:
by Phil Caroom, Maryland Matters November 26, 2025

by Phil Caroom, Maryland Matters November 26, 2025

Gov. Wes Moore’s September decision to close the aging Maryland Correctional Institute at Jessup, or MCIJ, was very good news. Why?  Because the state’s 12 other prisons don’t operate at full capacity.

With redistribution of correctional officers and incarcerated individuals, a smaller Maryland prison could work much more effectively. Our current arrangement is dangerously dysfunctional.

Maryland’s criminal justice system, in recent years, has see-sawed between tough-on-crime ideas, on one hand, that expand our prisons, and smarter ideas, on the other hand, that shrink the prisons – simultaneously, helping better to safeguard our communities.

Ten years ago, Maryland’s governor and legislators agreed on an important new bipartisan plan — the Justice Reinvestment Act (JRA). Study after study has shown that mere prison time does not reduce criminal activity upon release. So, JRA’s milestone, bipartisan plan aimed to shrink the state’s prison population and spend the tax savings on prevention measures proven to cut the crime rate.

Over the next few years, state prison populations shrank 23% and our crime rate dropped. But now, in the past two years, JRA’s plan faces a serious problem.

As of December 2024, Maryland’s prison administrators reported that they cannot hire correctional officers fast enough to replace those leaving (10.8% gap or 574 officers ). Completing fiscal year 2024, the population of incarcerated individuals was rising (a 3% rise or 560 more incarcerated people).  This is progress in the wrong direction.

Why should voters care? More than 90% of those in Maryland prisons will someday return to our communities. Their recidivism or law-abidingness correlate strongly to what happens while they are behind prison walls.

Those who complete their educations with GEDs or other degrees, those who learn marketable job skills, and those who get substance abuse treatment become much less likely to commit new offenses. Our communities get safer and healthier. And our taxpayer costs for prisons get smaller as prisons shrink.

But these protective measures (school, jobs, treatment — and more) all get canceled if there aren’t enough correctional officers to accompany  incarcerated individuals to prison classrooms.  As stated in Maryland prisons’ FY’26 budget overview, “CO [correctional officer] vacancies are particularly troubling as low staffing rates contribute to inmate idleness, safety risks, and a reduced emphasis on rehabilitation.”

For example, at Eastern Correctional Institute (ECI) this summer between late June and mid-September all prison classrooms were empty and prisoners  were locked in their cells nearly 23 hours per day, due to the shortage of correctional officers — while the temperatures regularly hit 100 degrees.

ECI isn’t the only Maryland prison with such problems.

There are proven, evidence-based solutions: One prison management system, used in seven other states (“Restoring Promise”), could reduce assaults among incarcerated individuals by 90%! Correctional officer satisfaction also greatly increases where this system is adopted. But Maryland hasn’t pursued this system yet, despite invitations over several years.

Increased use of “peer mentors” — well-trained, responsible older prisoners — also could help to counsel younger ones  and reduce the burden on prison staff. And it would provide job experience for these mentors when later released.

Increased pay for correctional officers might seem to increase the budget. But, in the long run, these dollars would reduce  mandatory overtime, reduce the quit-rate of experienced correctional officers, and reduce the need to continuously train new, inexperienced ones.

With Maryland’s state and local elections approaching in 2026, both voters and candidates should keep in mind that “tough on crime” may not be so smart, either for public safety or for our taxpayers’ burden.
